conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, the book's short-side wording is the mirror. Helpers: body(i)=|close[i]-open[i]|; range(i)=high[i]-low[i]; tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); ema(n) = XAverage(close, n); highest(x,n,k)/lowest(x,n,k) = extreme of x over n bars ending k bars ago (k=0 includes bar 0); barsSinceSessionOpen() = bars elapsed since today's first bar (intraday-only helper). This chapter is almost entirely discursive/conceptual with six chart-example figures (15.1-15.6); the figures narrate already-mined pattern vocabulary (final flag, wedge bull flag, ii pattern, 20 gap bar, double top/bottom, breakout pullback, measured move, two-legged pullback) rather than stating new mechanizable rules, so they were not re-mined bar-by-bar here.

candidates.name: StrongTrendBarPrimitive
candidates.quote: There usually has to have been at least two consecutive strong bull trend bars before most traders will believe that the always-in direction is long
candidates.description: Primitive: the current bar is a strong bull trend bar - bull close, body at least a fraction of its range, and small tails.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && body(0) >= bodyFraction * range(0) && (high[0] - close[0]) <= tailFraction * range(0) && (open[0] - low[0]) <= tailFraction * range(0)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used throughout the chapter's always-in tests)
notes: Same shape as V02-01 in this book's chapter 2; defined again here since this chapter's always-in tests depend on it directly.
Used via depends_on by most other candidates in this file.

candidates.name: AlwaysInDirection
candidates.quote: If you had to be in the market at all times, either long or short, the always-in position is whatever your current position is.
candidates.description: Primitive context concept: the market's presumed always-in direction, the side a trader would be forced to choose right now. Approximated as being above the EMA and above the close N bars ago (a proxy for 'the short-term trend'); Brooks explicitly says the true test is trader consensus, not a bar formula.

complexity.reason: the chapter's own definition is 'whatever a forced trader would choose right now', a consensus judgment; the EMA-plus-momentum test is one workable proxy, not Brooks's definition

notes: Same primitive as T00-01 (Trends front matter) and R01-?? (Ranges); this is the chapter that treats it as the central topic, so it is redefined here as the canonical reversals-book source.
The concrete flip tests V15-03..V15-10 are how the chapter actually operationalizes this concept.

candidates.name: AlwaysInFlipTwoConsecutiveStrongTrendBars
candidates.quote: There usually has to have been at least two consecutive strong bull trend bars before most traders will believe that the always-in direction is long, and at least two consecutive strong bear trend bars before they will think that always in is short.
candidates.description: The always-in direction flips to long when the current bar and the bar before it are both strong bull trend bars (consecutiveBars, default 2, is the tunable count Brooks calls 'two or more').
candidates.book_order_type: enter at the market or on the first pullback once the second consecutive trend bar closes

complexity.reason: a fixed-offset loop over the strong-trend-bar primitive, but treated as the chapter's core cross-bar always-in test

notes: This is the chapter's single most concrete, most repeated always-in test.
ConsecutiveUpBars tests close vs. own open with no size/tail requirement; this adds the strong-trend-bar shape.

candidates.name: AlwaysInFlipSingleTrendBarInContext
candidates.quote: If the context is right, even a single trend bar with an average range can be enough to make traders believe that the always-in position has flipped to the opposite direction.
candidates.description: A weaker, single-bar version of V15-03: one bull trend bar with a range near the average bar range can flip the always-in direction, but only when the surrounding context favors a reversal - a design decision Brooks leaves unspecified.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'if the context is right' has no bar-level definition in this chapter
close[0] > open[0] && range(0) >= rangeMultiple * avgRange(rangeLookback) && contextFavorsReversal[0]
candidates.book_order_type: enter at the market or on a small pullback

complexity.reason: 'if the context is right' is explicitly a judgment call with no bar-level test given; the single-bar size threshold alone is not what Brooks is describing

notes: Kept distinct from V15-03 because Brooks treats the one-bar and two-bar cases as different confidence levels, not the same test with N=1.

candidates.name: FollowThroughBarNoOppositeClose
candidates.quote: As a guideline, the minimum requirement for an always-in flip to short is usually that the follow-through bar not have a bull close ... The minimum requirement for the follow-through bar is usually that it does not have a bear close.
candidates.description: Minimum confirmation test: after a strong breakout bar (bar 1), the always-in direction flips only if the very next bar (bar 0, the follow-through bar) does not close in the opposite direction - i.e., after a strong bull breakout bar, the follow-through bar must not have a bear close.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (minimum confirmation test for an always-in flip)

complexity.reason: two-bar test combining the strong-trend-bar primitive on the prior bar with a close-color test on the current bar

notes: This is the weakest confirmation Brooks gives; V15-06 is the strong-confirmation form.

candidates.name: FollowThroughBarStrongContinuationEntry
candidates.quote: If the follow-through bar is strong, traders can enter on the close of the bar or on a small pullback. For example, if there is a strong bull breakout and the next bar is a strong bull trend bar, many traders will buy on the close of that follow-through bar or on a one- or two-tick pullback.
candidates.description: Strong confirmation: after a strong breakout bar, the follow-through bar is itself a strong same-direction trend bar - enter at its close (mechanized as next bar's open) or on a small pullback below its close.
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the follow-through bar, or on a limit order one or two ticks below its close

complexity.reason: two consecutive applications of the trivial strong-trend-bar primitive

notes: Equivalent to V15-03 with consecutiveBars=2; recorded separately because Brooks frames it as the entry-timing rule (close vs. small pullback), not the flip test itself.

candidates.name: FollowThroughBarWeakRequiresPullback
candidates.quote: If the follow-through bar is weak, like a doji, it is usually better to look to buy pullbacks rather than the close of the bar.
candidates.description: Filter: when the follow-through bar after a strong breakout bar is weak (small body relative to its range, i.e. not itself a strong trend bar), do not enter at its close - wait for a pullback entry instead.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (filter; suppresses the close-of-bar entry in favor of a pullback entry)

complexity.reason: two-bar test combining the strong-trend-bar primitive with a body-size threshold on the following bar

notes: Logical complement of V15-06's continuation condition; gates which entry style (close vs. pullback) applies.

candidates.name: FollowThroughExtensionBeyondBreakoutBar
candidates.quote: If the follow-through bar goes only a few ticks beyond the breakout bar, odds favor a failed breakout. If it goes many ticks beyond, the odds favor the bar becoming a strong trend bar once it closes.
candidates.description: The follow-through bar's high extends at least a threshold number of ticks beyond the breakout bar's high - odds favor the always-in direction confirming rather than the breakout failing.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (strength assessment of the follow-through bar in progress)

complexity.reason: two-bar price comparison against a tick threshold

notes: Brooks gives no numbers for 'a few' vs. 'many' ticks; extensionTicks is a reading of the distinction and should be optimized.

candidates.name: AlwaysInPersistsWithoutOppositeSpike
candidates.quote: if there is a bull breakout followed by a few weak bars of follow-through, and then the market begins to form a weak bear channel without ever having a bear spike, the market can remain always-in long.
candidates.description: Filter: after a bull breakout, the always-in direction remains long as long as no strong bear trend bar (a bear 'spike') has appeared within the lookback, even if price has pulled back for several bars in a shallow channel.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context persistence filter; traders keep protective stops in case the pullback grows)

complexity.reason: an absence-of-event test over a window of the strong-trend-bar primitive, plus cross-bar persistence of the prior always-in state

notes: Negative complement of V15-03/V15-09's mirror: a strong opposite trend bar is what would break this persistence and trigger a new flip test.

candidates.name: TightRangeDurationBreakoutMode
candidates.quote: At this point, the market had been in a tiny range for over 30 minutes, and when that happens, especially when there is a large gap opening, the market is in breakout mode. Traders would have placed buy stops at one tick above the high of the range and would go short on a stop at one tick below the low of the range.
candidates.description: When the range of the last N bars has stayed within a tight tolerance for at least that many bars, the market is in breakout mode: enter on a stop one tick beyond either side of that tight range.
candidates.pseudocode: isTightRange = (highest(high, durationBars, 1) - lowest(low, durationBars, 1)) <= rangeTicks * tick; close[0] > highest(high, durationBars, 1) && isTightRange
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the tight range's high (short: sell stop one tick below its low)

complexity.reason: a window highest/lowest range test plus a breakout comparison

notes: '30 minutes' is bar-count-dependent on the chart's timeframe; durationBars is the generalized parameter.
This chapter's tight-range breakout-mode test likely overlaps with the dedicated tight-trading-range chapter in the Ranges book.

candidates.name: AlwaysInBlocksCountertrendEntries
candidates.quote: If you believe that there is an always-in direction, you should not take countertrend trades.
candidates.description: Filter: once the always-in direction is established, only trade with that direction - a long entry is allowed only when the always-in direction is long, and vice versa.

complexity.reason: inherits the research-grade always-in primitive it gates on

notes: This is the plainest statement of the trilogy's most repeated filter (see V02-35 in this book's chapter 2); recorded again here since this chapter is the concept's canonical source.

candidates.name: ExitOnOppositeSignalWeakerThanReversal
candidates.quote: Traders will generally exit a trade on a signal in the opposite direction, even if that signal is not strong enough for them to reverse direction. Remember, it takes less to convince traders that it is time to exit a long than it does for them to take a short.
candidates.description: Exit a long on a single strong bear trend bar, even though flipping the always-in direction itself to short requires the stronger two-consecutive-bar test (V15-03) - exiting needs a weaker signal than reversing.
candidates.book_order_type: exit at the close of the opposite strong trend bar, or on a stop below it

complexity.reason: position-state gate combined with the trivial strong-trend-bar primitive

notes: The asymmetry (exit threshold lower than reversal threshold) is the mechanizable part; V15-03 supplies the reversal-strength comparison.

candidates.name: SecondPullbackToEntryStopOut
candidates.quote: In general, if there is a pullback that would have hit a breakeven stop and then the market resumes in your direction for several bars, it should not come back to your entry price again. Therefore, in most cases, you could then move your stop to breakeven. If it is hit by that second pullback and you are not certain of the market's direction, just remain flat.
candidates.description: Exit at breakeven the second time price returns to the entry price, provided the first return was followed by the market resuming in the trade's favor (moving away from entry by a margin) before coming back.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop at the entry price on the second qualifying pullback

complexity.reason: a persistent per-position counter/state machine across bars, tracking a first touch-and-recovery before arming the exit on a second touch

notes: Distinct from the simple breakeven-stop idea already mined as V02-16: this one requires two separate touches of entry with an intervening favorable move, not a single activation-then-breakeven test.
'Remain flat' afterward is just the absence of a new signal and needs no separate rule.

candidates.name: FirstHourTwoTrendBarScalpSetup
candidates.quote: During the first hour, before a clear trend is established, two consecutive bull trend bars will make traders look for buy scalps, and two consecutive bear trend bars will make them look for sell scalps.
candidates.description: The two-consecutive-strong-trend-bar always-in flip test (V15-03), restricted to the first N bars of the session and used for a scalp rather than a swing target.
candidates.book_order_type: enter at the market or on the first pullback, targeting a scalp rather than a full swing

complexity.reason: adds a session-time gate (bars since the session open) to the moderate V15-03 test

notes: firstHourBars is chart-timeframe-dependent; 12 assumes 5-minute bars for a 60-minute window and should be re-derived per timeframe.

candidates.name: AlwaysInConceptComposite
candidates.quote: This might be the single most important concept in trading. Traders should constantly assess whether the market is trending, and an "always-in" approach can help a trader to make that important determination.
candidates.description: Research-grade composite for the chapter's central concept: a persistent always-in direction state that starts undefined, flips on a two-strong-trend-bar breakout with adequate follow-through confirmation (no opposite close, adequate extension), persists through pullbacks that fail to produce an opposing strong trend bar, and blocks countertrend entries while it holds.

// research: state machine combining V15-02 (proxy direction), V15-03 (flip trigger), V15-05/V15-08 (confirmation strength), V15-09 (persistence), V15-11 (the resulting entry gate)
alwaysInLong[0] = (alwaysInLong[1] && !AlwaysInFlipTwoConsecutiveStrongTrendBars_bear[0]) || AlwaysInFlipTwoConsecutiveStrongTrendBars_bull[0];
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (the concept underlying every always-in entry in this chapter)

complexity.reason: the always-in direction is explicitly a design decision that composes several lower-grade tests into a persistent state machine; no single bar-level formula is authoritative

notes: This is the chapter's thesis; the authoring pass should decide whether to implement it as one stateful indicator/filter or leave it decomposed into V15-03/V15-05/V15-08/V15-09/V15-11 used directly.

chapter_summary: The trilogy's definition chapter for 'always-in', the presumed direction a trader would be forced to choose right now. Brooks gives several concrete, mechanizable tests for when that direction flips: two consecutive strong trend bars (the core test), a weaker single-bar-in-context version, a minimum follow-through-bar confirmation (no opposite close), a strong-confirmation continuation entry, a follow-through extension-in-ticks test, and a persistence filter (direction survives a pullback that never produces an opposing spike). It also gives a tight-range-duration breakout-mode test, a countertrend-blocking filter, an asymmetric exit-vs-reversal threshold, and a two-touch breakeven-stop exit. A research-grade composite ties these into the chapter's central state-machine concept. The six chart figures mostly re-illustrate pattern vocabulary (final flag, wedge bull flag, ii pattern, double top/bottom, breakout pullback) already mined in earlier chapters and were not re-mined bar-by-bar.
